intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Pallister-Hall-like syndrome (PHLS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous (bi-allelic) mutation in the SMO gene.

checks.claim: Pallister-Hall-like syndrome (PHLS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous (bi-allelic) mutation in the SMO gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we report bi-allelic loss-of-function variations in SMO in seven individuals from five independent families; these variations cause a wide phenotypic spectrum of developmental anomalies
checks.explanation: The abstract supports bi-allelic SMO variation as the cause. It does not use the name 'Pallister-Hall-like syndrome' and does not say whether the variants were homozygous or compound heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: Pallister-Hall-like syndrome is a developmental disorder caused by loss of SMO function. Its features vary widely. They include hypothalamic hamartoma and microcephaly; heart defects such as atrioventricular septal defect; skeletal anomalies including postaxial polydactyly, narrow chest and shortening of the long bones; and aganglionosis of the enteric nervous system (Le et al., 2020). Hypothalamic hamartoma with polydactyly in this condition resembles Pallister-Hall syndrome, which is caused by GLI3 mutation, but PHLS is a separate familial syndrome (Rubino et al., 2019).

checks.claim: Pallister-Hall-like syndrome is a developmental disorder caused by loss of SMO function.
checks.evidence_quote: Thus, loss of SMO function results in abnormal PC dynamics of key components of the Hh signaling pathway and leads to a large continuum of malformations in humans.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports a developmental disorder caused by loss of SMO function, but it never names it Pallister-Hall-like syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) proposed the name 'congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome' (CHHS) for a possibly familial entity. In their definition, the minimum criteria were skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities occurring with congenital hypothalamic hamartoma.

checks.claim: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) proposed the name 'congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome' (CHHS) for a possibly familial entity.
checks.evidence_quote: a nosologically distinct, possibly familial entity, which we suggest calling "congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome" (CHHS).
checks.explanation: The abstract states the proposed name directly.

checks.claim: In the definition of congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome by Encha-Razavi et al. (1992), the minimum criteria were skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities occurring with congenital hypothalamic hamartoma.
checks.evidence_quote: These findings prompt us to consider skeletal dysplasia and oro-facial abnormalities as common denominator and minimum criteria required to define a nosologically distinct, possibly familial entity, which we suggest calling "congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome" (CHHS).
checks.explanation: Skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities are named as the minimum criteria. The hamartoma is part of the syndrome by definition.

paragraphs.text: Marcuse et al. (1953) reported 2 cases of hypothalamic hamartoma with associated developmental defects. Only the title of this report was available.

checks.explanation: The title says the paper reports two cases of hypothalamic hamartoma with associated developmental defects, which is exactly what the claim states.

paragraphs.text: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) found congenital hypothalamic hamartomas at autopsy in 3 unrelated fetuses. In the first 2, the tumor occurred with skeletal dysplasia alone. In the third, it was part of a nonrandom pattern of congenital malformations suggestive of Meckel syndrome. In 1 family, an earlier-born boy had died soon after birth with similar craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities. The authors reviewed published cases of Pallister-Hall syndrome and found that only skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities were consistently present. They proposed these features as the minimum criteria for a distinct, possibly familial entity, which they called 'congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome' (CHHS).

checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly. 'Similar' refers to the fetus in that family.

paragraphs.text: Rubino et al. (2019) described 2 brothers with a familial syndrome of hypothalamic hamartomas and polydactyly. In 1 brother, a large hypothalamic hamartoma underwent endoscopic endonasal biopsy and subtotal resection.

paragraphs.text: Le et al. (2020) reported 7 affected individuals from 5 independent families. Their developmental anomalies spanned a wide range. Brain findings were hypothalamic hamartoma and microcephaly, and the heart defect was atrioventricular septal defect. Skeletal findings were postaxial polydactyly, narrow chest and shortening of the long bones. The enteric nervous system showed aganglionosis.

checks.evidence_quote: we report bi-allelic loss-of-function variations in SMO in seven individuals from five independent families
checks.explanation: The counts of 7 individuals and 5 families match. The abstract does not use the label Pallister-Hall-like syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Le et al. (2020) found bi-allelic SMO mutations in affected individuals from 5 families, which is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Rubino et al. (2019) had earlier described the disorder in 2 affected brothers.

checks.evidence_quote: we report bi-allelic loss-of-function variations in SMO in seven individuals from five independent families
checks.explanation: The abstract states bi-allelic SMO variants in affected individuals from 5 families.

checks.claim: The bi-allelic SMO mutations found by Le et al. (2020) are consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance of Pallister-Hall-like syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: we report bi-allelic loss-of-function variations in SMO in seven individuals from five independent families
checks.explanation: Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants imply recessive inheritance, but the abstract never says 'autosomal recessive'. It also does not name the disorder Pallister-Hall-like syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Rubino et al. (2019) found germline mutations in the SMO gene in 2 brothers with hypothalamic hamartomas and polydactyly. The authors stated that this was the first report of a familial syndrome caused by germline SMO mutations. The abstract did not give the specific variants or their zygosity.

checks.explanation: The title confirms the features: hypothalamic hamartomas, polydactyly and SMO mutations in two cases (the brothers).

paragraphs.text: Le et al. (2020) identified bi-allelic loss-of-function mutations in the SMO gene in 7 individuals from 5 independent families. Cells derived from affected individuals formed cilia normally, but hedgehog signal transduction was severely altered. This resulted either from altered trafficking at the primary cilium or from abnormal activation of the pathway downstream of SMO. In cells from affected individuals, GLI2 also accumulated at the tip of the primary cilium independently of hedgehog. This finding suggested that SMO may regulate basal ciliary trafficking of GLI2 when the pathway is off.

agent.process_note: I read all 5 files in full. Only abstracts were available, and for Marcuse et al. (1953) only the title. No specific SMO variants (nucleotide or protein changes), zygosity for individual patients, ancestry or consanguinity appear in the abstracts, so no allelic variants were entered. The reference data did not supply a MIM number or chromosomal location for SMO, so both are left out of the intro. Craig et al. (2008) deals with somatic GLI3 abnormalities in sporadic nonsyndromic hypothalamic hamartoma, not with this syndrome, so I left it uncited.
